The top of printed p. 21 sits beside a photograph and is missing from the text layer, so it was read on the page image

bibliography.checked_against: the report's cover/title page (PDF p. 2) and the UW library record (PDF p. 1)
bibliography.corrections: the second author is 'Jerry L. Pederson Jr.' on the title page (add 'Jr.'); Wisconsin DNR Research Report 177 is dated December 1998
bibliography.note: title, year, series and number match: 'The Construction, Aesthetics, and Effects of Lakeshore Development: A Literature Review', Research Report 177, Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources; Sandy Engel (Bureau of Integrated Science Services) and Jerry L. Pederson Jr. (UW–Stevens Point)

claims.claim: Fish use piers for shade but rarely to feed or nest
claims.quote: used by nearshore fishes for shade and shelter but rarely for feeding and nesting
claims.conditions: a literature review (276 works, 1919–98), mostly Wisconsin and other Midwest lakes; the statement is the reviewers' synthesis, supported in the same paragraph by Colle et al. 1989 (Florida: piers preferred by 4 of 27 radio-tagged largemouth bass after grass carp removed the plant beds, but 'seldom lingered') and Helfman 1979/1981 (floating boards in a New York lake)
claims.note: the source's reason: these structures 'lack the structural complexity of plant beds, rocky substrates, and woody debris'

claims.claim: bluegill and pumpkinseed > 12 cm, perch, bass and suckers showed no attraction to floating boards
claims.location: p. 21 (PDF p. 24), first column (read on the page image)
claims.quote: Bluegills and pumpkinseed sunfish more than 4.7 inches in total length
claims.conditions: Helfman 1979, as reviewed here: floating boards in a New York lake; 4.7 in = 11.9 cm TOTAL length; the no-attraction group was bluegill and pumpkinseed > 4.7 in and 'all rock bass, largemouth bass, yellow perch, and white suckers'; the attracted sunfish were 3.1–4.7 in (7.9–11.9 cm) TL; black crappies and golden shiners were attracted but hovered just outside the boards
claims.note: the 'bass' are rock bass and largemouth bass (the sim applies it to smallmouth); smaller sunfish (< 3.1 in, 7.9 cm) were not reported on, so the sim's 'under DOCK_L' (all sizes below 12 cm) extends the finding downward. Cite as 'Helfman 1979, via Engel & Pederson 1998'

claims.claim: "shade and shelter by day, not feeding or nesting" (given in quotation marks)
claims.source_value: the source's words are 'used by nearshore fishes for shade and shelter but rarely for feeding and nesting'
claims.quote: shade and shelter but rarely for feeding and nesting
claims.note: the comment's quotation is not verbatim: the source says 'rarely', not 'not', and does not say 'by day' (its time-of-day evidence is the separate Helfman board study, next claim). Paraphrase without quotation marks, or quote it exactly

claims.claim: small sunfish hover in the dock's shade only while the sun is high and the sky clear: 'weight 0 at night, under cloud'
claims.source_value: fish densities under the boards were highest around noon on sunny days, MODERATE on overcast days and lowest at night (range 1.1–7.7 fish/ft²) — not zero under cloud
claims.location: p. 21 (PDF p. 24), first column (read on the page image)
claims.quote: highest around noon on sunny days, moderate on overcast days, and lowest at night
claims.conditions: Helfman 1979, floating boards in a New York lake, as reviewed here; 3.1–4.7-in bluegill and pumpkinseed
claims.note: the quoted rule 'weight 0 at night, under cloud' is the project's (research note 'Values for the sim'), not the source's; the source gives a graded response (overcast = moderate). It also notes that shade structures 'do not always attract fishes in full sunlight' (Lake Tahoe: no preference at any of 70 piers in a low-water year, Beauchamp et al. 1994) and that shade is weaker in turbid water

claims.claim: a fish under floating shade sees a predator at 2.7× the distance at which the predator sees it (Helfman 1981)
claims.source_value: 'can see predators UP TO 2.7 times the visual distance that predators can see the prey' — a maximum, not a typical ratio
claims.quote: can see predators up to 2.7 times the visual distance that predators can see
claims.note: the comment cites Helfman 1981 directly; the text read here is Engel & Pederson's summary of it, which gives 2.7 as an upper value. Unless Helfman 1981 is read and gives 2.7 as a mean, cite 'Helfman 1981, via Engel & Pederson 1998' and treat DOCK_COVER as an upper bound

notes: The paper's own sentence (§3.2.9) checks; the corrections are in the code comment's wording and in how the Helfman board data are read (graded with cloud, 'up to' 2.7×). Other dockage material on pp. 20–21: Colle et al. 1989 (Florida largemouth bass and piers after grass carp); 1.1–7.7 fish/ft² under the boards; crappies and golden shiners hovered just outside the boards; piers cast most shade close to the water and less when water is turbid or low; plant beds, rock outcrops, boulder spits and woody debris draw fish away from piers despite shade. The same pages cover woody-debris removal (pumpkinseed nesting on cleared areas, Colgan & Ealey 1973) and turbidity effects on young fish feeding.
